content.heading: 5.3 Diagonalization
content.paragraph: In many cases, the eigenvalue–eigenvector information contained within a matrix $A$ can be displayed in a useful factorization of the form $A = PDP^{- 1}$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. In this section, the factorization enables us to compute $A^{k}$ quickly for large values of $k$, a fundamental idea in several applications of linear algebra. Later, in Sections 5.6 and 5.7, the factorization will be used to analyze (and decouple) dynamical systems.

content.paragraph: A square matrix $A$ is said to be diagonalizable if $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix, that is, if $A = PDP^{- 1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and some diagonal matrix $D$. The next theorem gives a characterization of diagonalizable matrices and tells how to construct a suitable factorization.

note.title: Theorem ﻿5
note.heading: Theorem ﻿5
The Diagonalization Theorem﻿
note.paragraph: An $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

In fact, $A = PDP^{- 1}$, with $D$ a diagonal matrix, if and only if the columns of $P$ are $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$. In this case, the diagonal entries of $D$ are eigenvalues of $A$ that correspond, respectively, to the eigenvectors in $P$.

content.paragraph: In other words, $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if there are enough eigenvectors to form a basis of $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$. We call such a basis an eigenvector basis of $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$.
content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: First, observe that if $P$ is any $n \times n$ matrix with columns $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$, and if $D$ is any diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$, then
Now suppose $A$ is diagonalizable and $A = PDP^{- 1}$. Then right-multiplying this relation by $P$, we have $AP = PD$. In this case, equations (1) and (2) imply that

Since $P$ is invertible, its columns $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$ must be linearly independent. Also, since these columns are nonzero, the equations in (4) show that $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$ are eigenvalues and $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$ are corresponding eigenvectors. This argument proves the “only if” parts of the first and second statements, along with the third statement, of the theorem.

Finally, given any $n$ eigenvectors $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$, use them to construct the columns of $P$ and use corresponding eigenvalues $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$ to construct $D$. By equations (1)–(3), $AP = PD$. This is true without any condition on the eigenvectors. If, in fact, the eigenvectors are linearly independent, then $P$ is invertible (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem), and $AP = PD$ implies that $A = PDP^{- 1}$.

content.paragraph: The following theorem provides a sufficient condition for a matrix to be diagonalizable.

note.title: Theorem 6
note.heading: Theorem 6
note.paragraph: An $n \times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: Let $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$ be eigenvectors corresponding to the $n$ distinct eigenvalues of a matrix $A$. Then $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$ is linearly independent, by Theorem 2 in Section 5.1. Hence $A$ is diagonalizable, by Theorem 5.

It is not necessary for an $n \times n$ matrix to have $n$ distinct eigenvalues in order to be diagonalizable. The $3 \times 3$ matrix in Example 3 is diagonalizable even though it has only two distinct eigenvalues.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Determine if the following matrix is diagonalizable.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: This is easy! Since the matrix is triangular, its eigenvalues are obviously $5$, $0$, and $- 2$. Since $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with three distinct eigenvalues, $A$ is diagonalizable.

content.heading: Matrices Whose Eigenvalues Are Not Distinct

note.title: Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix whose distinct eigenvalues are $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{p}$.

list.item: For 1≤k≤p, the dimension of the eigenspace for λk is less than or equal to the multiplicity of the eigenvalue λk.

The matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces equals n, and this happens if and only if (i) the characteristic polynomial factors completely into linear factors and (ii) the dimension of the eigenspace for each λk equals the multiplicity of λk.
If A is diagonalizable and Bk is a basis for the eigenspace corresponding to λk for each k, then the total collection of vectors in the sets B1,…,Bp forms an eigenvector basis for ℝn.
